notes.front: What is an event in Scrum, in one sentence?
notes.back: A formal opportunity to inspect and adapt the artifacts; Scrum has five, and the Sprint contains the other four.
notes.explanation: Events create regularity and minimise the need for meetings Scrum does not define.
notes.example: Like fixed check-ups at a clinic: scheduled, each with a clear purpose, rather than ad hoc visits.

notes.front: What does it mean that a Scrum event is timeboxed?
notes.back: It has a maximum duration that it must not exceed.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Master ensures that events are kept within their timebox.
notes.example: Like a 15-minute parking bay: you can leave early, but you cannot stay longer.

notes.front: What is Sprint Planning, in one sentence?
notes.back: The event that starts the Sprint by laying out the work to be performed, created by the whole Scrum Team.
notes.explanation: It produces the Sprint Goal and the rest of the Sprint Backlog.
notes.example: Like a crew’s briefing before a voyage: why we are going, where to, and how.

notes.front: What is the Daily Scrum, in one sentence?
notes.back: A 15-minute event for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog.
notes.explanation: It produces an actionable plan for the next day of work.
notes.example: Like a kitchen’s quick huddle before service: where are we, and what do we change next?

notes.front: What is the Sprint Review, in one sentence?
notes.back: The event where the Scrum Team and key stakeholders inspect the Sprint’s outcome and decide future adaptations.
notes.explanation: Progress toward the Product Goal is discussed, and the Product Backlog may be adjusted.
notes.example: Like a test screening: the audience sees the film so far, and the edit changes with what everyone learns.

notes.front: What is the Sprint Retrospective, in one sentence?
notes.back: The event where the Scrum Team plans ways to increase quality and effectiveness; it concludes the Sprint.
notes.explanation: It inspects how the last Sprint went: individuals, interactions, processes, tools and the Definition of Done.
notes.example: Like a sports team watching its match footage to change how it plays next time.

notes.front: Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of {{c1::eight hours}} for a one-month Sprint.
notes.explanation: For shorter Sprints, the event is usually shorter.

notes.front: The Daily Scrum is a {{c1::15}}-minute event.
notes.explanation: It is held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint, to reduce complexity.

notes.front: The Sprint Review is timeboxed to a maximum of {{c1::four hours}} for a one-month Sprint.
notes.explanation: For shorter Sprints, the event is usually shorter.

notes.front: The Sprint Retrospective is timeboxed to a maximum of {{c1::three hours}} for a one-month Sprint.
notes.explanation: For shorter Sprints, the event is usually shorter.

notes.front: Which three topics does Sprint Planning address?
notes.back: Why is this Sprint valuable? What can be Done this Sprint? How will the chosen work get done?
notes.explanation: Why becomes the Sprint Goal, what becomes the selected items, and how becomes the plan: together, the Sprint Backlog.

notes.front: In Sprint Planning, who proposes how the product could increase its value in the current Sprint?
notes.back: The Product Owner.
notes.explanation: The whole Scrum Team then collaborates to define a Sprint Goal.

notes.front: By when must the Sprint Goal be finalised?
notes.back: Before the end of Sprint Planning.
notes.explanation: It is created in Sprint Planning and then added to the Sprint Backlog.

notes.front: Who selects the Product Backlog items for the Sprint?
notes.back: The Developers, through discussion with the Product Owner.
notes.explanation: The more the Developers know about their past performance, capacity and Definition of Done, the more confident their forecast.

notes.front: Who decides how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments?
notes.back: The Developers alone: no one else tells them how.
notes.explanation: How this is done is at the sole discretion of the Developers.

notes.front: Who participates in the Daily Scrum?
notes.back: The Developers. The Product Owner or Scrum Master participate as Developers if they are actively working on Sprint Backlog items.
notes.explanation: It is an event for the Developers of the Scrum Team.

notes.front: Is the Daily Scrum the only time the Developers may adjust their plan?
notes.back: No. They often meet throughout the day to adapt or re-plan the rest of the Sprint’s work.
notes.explanation: The Daily Scrum gives a fixed daily point, but it is not a limit.

notes.front: The Sprint Review is the {{c1::second to last}} event of the Sprint.
notes.explanation: The Sprint Retrospective comes after it and concludes the Sprint.

notes.front: What does the Scrum Team inspect in the Sprint Retrospective?
notes.back: How the last Sprint went: individuals, interactions, processes, tools and the Definition of Done.
notes.explanation: It identifies the most helpful changes to improve its effectiveness.

notes.front: What may happen to the most impactful improvements identified in a Sprint Retrospective?
notes.back: They are addressed as soon as possible, and may even be added to the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint.
notes.explanation: Improvements are part of the work, not an afterthought.

notes.front: Who can cancel a Sprint?
notes.back: Only the Product Owner.
notes.explanation: A Sprint could be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.

notes.front: During a Sprint, which changes are ruled out?
notes.back: Any change that would endanger the Sprint Goal.
notes.explanation: Quality does not decrease either, but scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned.

notes.front: Why are Scrum events ideally held at the same time and place?
notes.back: To reduce complexity.
notes.explanation: Regular events also minimise the need for meetings Scrum does not define.

notes.front: Besides the Scrum Team, who may attend Sprint Planning?
notes.back: Other people the Scrum Team invites to provide advice.
notes.explanation: The whole Scrum Team creates the plan; guests only advise.

notes.front: Mid-Sprint, a stakeholder asks the Developers to swap in urgent work that would make the Sprint Goal impossible. What does Scrum say?
notes.back: No change is made that would endanger the Sprint Goal. If the goal becomes obsolete, only the Product Owner can cancel the Sprint.
notes.choices:
A) The Developers swap it in
B) The Scrum Master cancels the Sprint
C) Protect the Sprint Goal; only the Product Owner can cancel the Sprint
notes.choicesExplained: A: that would endanger the Sprint Goal. B: only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel a Sprint.
notes.explanation: The stakeholder can take the request to the Product Owner, who orders the Product Backlog.

notes.front: The Daily Scrum has become a 45-minute status report to a manager. What does the Scrum Guide say it should be?
notes.back: A 15-minute event for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and plan the next day’s work.
notes.explanation: The Developers choose its structure, as long as it focuses on the Sprint Goal and produces an actionable plan.

notes.front: A team runs its Sprint Review as a slide show with no discussion. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: It is a working session: the Scrum Team and stakeholders collaborate on what to do next.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Team should avoid limiting the Sprint Review to a presentation.

notes.front: Which event is this: the Scrum Team discusses what went well, what problems it hit, and how they were or were not solved?
notes.back: The Sprint Retrospective.
notes.explanation: The Sprint Retrospective looks at how the team worked, to increase quality and effectiveness.

notes.front: Which event is this: stakeholders see what was accomplished, and the Product Backlog may be adjusted?
notes.back: The Sprint Review.
notes.explanation: The Sprint Review inspects the outcome of the Sprint and determines future adaptations.

notes.front: Sprint Planning for a one-month Sprint runs for a day and a half. Is that within the timebox?
notes.back: No. Sprint Planning is at most eight hours for a one-month Sprint.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Master ensures events are kept within their timebox.

notes.front: A team holds back a Done, usable feature until the Sprint Review. Does Scrum require that?
notes.back: No. The Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value.
notes.explanation: An Increment may be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint.

notes.front: The Product Owner is not working on any Sprint Backlog items. Do they participate in the Daily Scrum as one of the Developers?
notes.back: No. The Product Owner participates as a Developer only when actively working on Sprint Backlog items.
notes.explanation: The Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers of the Scrum Team.

notes.front: What is the difference between the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective?
notes.back: Review: the outcome of the Sprint, with stakeholders. Retrospective: how the Scrum Team worked, to improve it.
notes.explanation: Both inspect and adapt, but different things: the product versus the way of working.
notes.contrast: The Review looks at what was built; the Retrospective at how it was built.
